title: C.4 Standing waves and resonance
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: C.4 Standing waves and resonance — IB Diploma Programme Physics (guide first assessment 2025, updated November 2023), topic C.4.
meta_desc: IB DP Physics practice covering C.4 Standing waves and resonance, guide topic C.4.
final_note: You worked through C.4 Standing waves and resonance — 6 guide statements.

concepts.def: A wave pattern formed by the superposition of two identical travelling waves (same frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed) moving in opposite directions through the same medium, usually an incident wave and its reflection. The pattern does not travel: the positions of the nodes and antinodes are fixed. Every point between the nodes oscillates, with an amplitude that depends on its position.

When two waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the displacements that each wave would produce on its own. In a standing wave the two travelling waves pass through each other unchanged; their displacements simply add at every point and every instant.

The two travelling waves carry energy at equal rates in opposite directions, so a standing wave produces no net transfer of energy along the medium. The energy stays within each section between nodes, changing between kinetic energy (greatest when the medium passes through its undisplaced position) and elastic potential energy (greatest at maximum displacement). Nodes never move, so no energy passes through them.

A point on a standing wave at which the displacement is zero at all times, because the two travelling waves always arrive there in antiphase and cancel. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength (λ/2) apart.

A point on a standing wave at which the amplitude of oscillation is greatest. If each travelling wave has amplitude A, the amplitude at an antinode is 2A. Adjacent antinodes are λ/2 apart, and each antinode lies midway between two nodes, λ/4 from each.

concepts.term: Relative amplitude along a standing wave
concepts.def: In a standing wave, unlike a travelling wave, the amplitude varies with position: it is zero at the nodes, greatest (2A) at the antinodes and takes intermediate values in between. Points at the same distance from a node have equal amplitudes.

concepts.term: Phase difference in a standing wave
concepts.def: All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase: they reach their maximum displacements at the same instant. Points in adjacent sections (on opposite sides of a node) oscillate in antiphase, a phase difference of π rad. The phase does not change steadily with distance as it does along a travelling wave.

A fixed end of a string cannot move, so it is always a displacement node. A free end (for example, a light ring sliding on a smooth rod) moves with the greatest amplitude, so it is a displacement antinode. The three cases are two fixed boundaries (node at each end), one fixed and one free boundary (node at one end, antinode at the other), and two free boundaries (antinode at each end).

concepts.term: Boundary conditions for air in pipes
concepts.def: Sound in air is longitudinal, so the air oscillates along the length of the pipe. At a closed end the air cannot move along the pipe, so a closed end is a displacement node. At an open end the air moves with the greatest amplitude, so an open end is a displacement antinode. Sound reflects at both kinds of end, so standing waves form in pipes with two closed ends, one closed and one open end, or two open ends.

The first harmonic is the lowest-frequency mode of a standing wave in a given string or pipe. A higher mode whose frequency is n times that of the first harmonic is the nth harmonic. Which values of n exist depends on the boundary conditions.

concepts.term: Harmonics with the same kind of boundary at both ends
concepts.def: For a string with two fixed or two free ends, or air in a pipe with two closed or two open ends, the length L holds a whole number of half-wavelengths. The nth harmonic has λ_n = 2L/n and f_n = v/λ_n = nv/(2L), where v is the wave speed, and every whole number n = 1, 2, 3, … occurs.

concepts.term: Harmonics with different boundaries at the two ends
concepts.def: For a string with one fixed and one free end, or air in a pipe closed at one end and open at the other, there is a node at one end and an antinode at the other, so L holds an odd number of quarter-wavelengths. The nth harmonic has λ_n = 4L/n and f_n = nv/(4L) with n odd only (1, 3, 5, …). The mode above the first harmonic is therefore the third harmonic, at three times the first-harmonic frequency.

The frequency at which a system oscillates when it is displaced and released and left to oscillate freely, with no periodic driving force. SI unit: Hz. A string or air column has a whole series of natural frequencies, one for each harmonic.

When a periodic external force acts on a system, the system is forced to oscillate. Once the initial transient motion has died away, it oscillates at the driving frequency (the frequency of the external force), not at its own natural frequency. The amplitude of this steady oscillation depends on how close the driving frequency is to the natural frequency.

The large increase in the amplitude of a forced oscillation that occurs when the driving frequency equals (for a lightly damped system, very nearly equals) a natural frequency of the system. The driving force then does positive work on the system throughout each cycle, so energy builds up until the energy supplied per cycle equals the energy dissipated per cycle by damping.

concepts.term: Useful and destructive effects of resonance
concepts.def: Useful: the tuned circuit of a radio receiver is adjusted so its natural frequency matches one station's frequency; a quartz crystal in a clock or watch is kept oscillating at its natural frequency to keep time; the air columns and strings of musical instruments resonate to produce loud notes. Destructive: a glass shattered by a sustained note at its natural frequency; buildings shaken by earthquake waves at a natural frequency of the building; machine parts, vehicle panels or washing machines that vibrate violently at particular engine or drum speeds; bridges and walkways set swaying by periodic forces from wind or walkers.

The removal of energy from an oscillating system by resistive forces (such as friction or air resistance), which transfer the energy to the internal energy of the system and its surroundings. For a driven oscillator, damping limits the amplitude at resonance.

concepts.term: Effect of damping on the frequency response
concepts.def: A graph of steady amplitude against driving frequency (the frequency response) has a peak near the natural frequency. As the damping increases, the maximum amplitude decreases, the peak becomes wider, and the frequency at which it occurs moves slightly lower. Far from the natural frequency the amplitude is almost unaffected by damping.

Damping small enough that the displaced system oscillates about equilibrium with an amplitude that decreases gradually over many cycles. The time period stays almost constant as the amplitude decreases (it is very slightly longer than with no damping).

The smallest degree of damping at which a displaced system returns to equilibrium without oscillating. It brings the system to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without passing through the equilibrium position; it is used in car suspensions, door closers and meter needles.
Damping greater than critical. The displaced system does not oscillate but returns to equilibrium slowly, taking longer than with critical damping; the heavier the damping, the slower the return.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a standing wave on a string is correct?
options: It forms where two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose.
It is a single wave that has stopped travelling, so its crests stay in fixed places.
It carries energy along the string from the source towards the far end.
Each point oscillates slightly later than its neighbour nearer the source.
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
mcqs.explain: A standing wave is the superposition of two waves with the same frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed moving in opposite directions, on a string usually the incident wave and its reflection. Their displacements add at every point, producing fixed nodes and antinodes.
rationales: A standing wave is the superposition of two waves with the same frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed moving in opposite directions, on a string usually the incident wave and its reflection. Their displacements add at every point, producing fixed nodes and antinodes.

A student who takes "standing" literally picks this. No crest stays in place: each antinode moves from a crest to a trough and back every cycle. The pattern is fixed because two travelling waves pass through each other.

A student who applies "waves transfer energy" to every wave picks this. The two component waves carry energy at equal rates in opposite directions, so a standing wave has no net energy transfer along the string.

A student who carries the travelling-wave idea of a steadily changing phase over to standing waves picks this. All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase, and points on opposite sides of a node are in antiphase.

mcqs.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its first harmonic. At one instant every point on the string has zero displacement, so the string is straight. Which statement about the string at this instant is correct?
options: Every point is momentarily at rest; its energy is all stored as elastic potential energy.
The two waves have cancelled each other out, so the string holds no energy at this instant.
Energy is being carried along the string from one fixed end to the other.
Points between the ends are moving at their greatest speeds; its energy is all kinetic.
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
mcqs.explain: Each point on the string oscillates about its undisplaced position and passes through it at its greatest speed. When the whole string is straight, every point except the fixed ends is at maximum speed, so the energy of the standing wave is all kinetic energy at this instant.
rationales: A student who thinks zero displacement means zero velocity picks this. Rest occurs at maximum displacement. A point passing through its undisplaced position is moving at its greatest speed, and a straight string has no extra stretch to store energy.

A student who thinks waves that cancel have destroyed each other picks this. Superposition adds displacements, not energies: the velocities do not cancel, so the energy is all kinetic, and the string is displaced again a quarter of a period later.

A student who thinks every wave transfers energy along the medium picks this. The two component waves carry energy equally in opposite directions, so the standing wave has no net energy transfer; the energy stays in the vibrating string.

Each point on the string oscillates about its undisplaced position and passes through it at its greatest speed. When the whole string is straight, every point except the fixed ends is at maximum speed, so the energy of the standing wave is all kinetic energy at this instant.

mcqs.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave. Its nodes are at x = 0, 0.40 m, 0.80 m and 1.20 m, measured from one end. Points P, Q and R on the string are at x = 0.10 m, 0.20 m and 0.70 m. Which statement about the oscillations of P, Q and R is correct?
options: P and Q oscillate π/4 rad out of phase, being λ/8 apart.
P and Q oscillate in phase, with amplitudes equal to each other.
P and R oscillate in antiphase, with equal amplitudes.
P and R oscillate in phase, with equal amplitudes.
mcqs.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
mcqs.explain: P (0.10 m) is 0.10 m from the node at 0, and R (0.70 m) is 0.10 m from the node at 0.80 m, so they have equal amplitudes. P lies between the nodes at 0 and 0.40 m, and R between the nodes at 0.40 m and 0.80 m: they are in adjacent sections, on opposite sides of the node at 0.40 m, so they oscillate in antiphase (phase difference π rad).
rationales: A student who uses the travelling-wave rule Δφ = 2πx/λ picks this: λ = 0.80 m and x = 0.10 m give π/4 rad. In a standing wave, P and Q lie between the same pair of nodes (0 and 0.40 m), so they oscillate in phase.

A student who thinks every point of a standing wave has the same amplitude picks this. P and Q are in phase, but Q is an antinode (maximum amplitude) while P, halfway between a node and the antinode, has a smaller amplitude.

P (0.10 m) is 0.10 m from the node at 0, and R (0.70 m) is 0.10 m from the node at 0.80 m, so they have equal amplitudes. P lies between the nodes at 0 and 0.40 m, and R between the nodes at 0.40 m and 0.80 m: they are in adjacent sections, on opposite sides of the node at 0.40 m, so they oscillate in antiphase (phase difference π rad).

A student who thinks the whole standing wave moves up and down together picks this. P and R do have equal amplitudes (each is 0.10 m from a node), but they are on opposite sides of the node at 0.40 m, so when P is displaced upwards R is displaced downwards: they are in antiphase.

mcqs.q: A vibrator of frequency 320 Hz sets up a standing wave on a stretched string. The distance between adjacent nodes is 0.45 m. What is the speed of the travelling waves on the string?
options: 144 m s⁻¹
288 m s⁻¹
576 m s⁻¹
356 m s⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
mcqs.explain: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 × 0.90 = 288 m s⁻¹.
mcqs.working: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 2 × 0.45 m = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 Hz × 0.90 m = 288 m s⁻¹.
rationales: A student who takes one loop (node to node) as a whole wavelength uses λ = 0.45 m and gets 320 × 0.45 = 144 m s⁻¹. Each loop is half a wavelength, so λ = 0.90 m.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 × 0.90 = 288 m s⁻¹.
A student who thinks adjacent nodes are λ/4 apart uses λ = 4 × 0.45 = 1.80 m and gets 576 m s⁻¹. A quarter-wavelength is the node-to-antinode distance; adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart.
A student who writes v = f/λ gets 320/0.90 = 356. The units of f/λ are s⁻¹ m⁻¹, not m s⁻¹. The wave equation is v = fλ = 288 m s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: A pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Where along the pipe is the displacement of the air zero at all times?
options: At the closed end of the pipe
Midway between the two ends
At both ends of the pipe
At no point along the pipe
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: A point where the displacement is zero at all times is a displacement node. The air at the closed end cannot move along the pipe, so it is a node; the air at the open end moves with the greatest amplitude, so it is an antinode. The first harmonic is the simplest pattern with a node at one end and an antinode at the other (L = λ/4), so the closed end is the only node.
rationales: A point where the displacement is zero at all times is a displacement node. The air at the closed end cannot move along the pipe, so it is a node; the air at the open end moves with the greatest amplitude, so it is an antinode. The first harmonic is the simplest pattern with a node at one end and an antinode at the other (L = λ/4), so the closed end is the only node.

A student who pictures the air hitting the closed end hardest treats that end as an antinode, so has antinodes at both ends and puts the node between them. The solid end stops the air next to it moving, so the closed end is a displacement node, and the open end is the only antinode.

A student who thinks every end is a node, as for a guitar string, picks this. Only the closed end is a node. The air at the open end is free to move and oscillates with the greatest amplitude: it is a displacement antinode.

A student who thinks every point of a standing wave oscillates with the same amplitude expects no point to be still. The amplitude varies along the pipe: zero at the closed end, where the air cannot move (a node), and greatest at the open end (an antinode).

mcqs.q: A string of length 0.80 m is fixed at both ends. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the third harmonic?
options: 450 Hz
900 Hz
300 Hz
150 Hz
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: With a node at each fixed end, the third harmonic has three loops, each λ/2 long: λ₃ = 2L/3 = 2 × 0.80/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240/0.533 = 450 Hz (equivalently 3 × 150 Hz).
mcqs.working: Two fixed ends: λ_n = 2L/n. λ₃ = 2 × 0.80 m/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240 m s⁻¹/0.533 m = 450 Hz. (Check: f₁ = v/2L = 240/1.60 = 150 Hz, and f₃ = 3f₁ = 450 Hz.)
rationales: With a node at each fixed end, the third harmonic has three loops, each λ/2 long: λ₃ = 2L/3 = 2 × 0.80/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240/0.533 = 450 Hz (equivalently 3 × 150 Hz).
A student who takes each loop as a whole wavelength uses λ = 0.80/3 = 0.267 m and gets 900 Hz. Each loop is half a wavelength, so λ₃ = 2L/3 = 0.533 m and f₃ = 450 Hz.

A student who thinks the third harmonic has three nodes, counting the ends, draws two loops and gets λ = 0.80 m, f = 300 Hz. That pattern is the second harmonic. The third harmonic has three loops and four nodes.

A student who thinks a string has only one natural frequency gives the first-harmonic value, 240/1.60 = 150 Hz. The third harmonic has one-third of the wavelength and, at the same wave speed, three times the frequency: 450 Hz.

mcqs.q: A string of length 0.60 m is fixed at one end. Its other end is free: it is tied to a light ring that slides without friction on a vertical rod. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. Which gives the harmonic number n, the wavelength λ and the frequency f of the standing wave with the next frequency above that of the first harmonic?
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: There is a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end, so L holds an odd number of quarter-wavelengths. The first harmonic has λ = 4L = 2.40 m and f₁ = 100 Hz. The next mode has L = 3λ/4, so λ = 0.80 m and f = 240/0.80 = 300 Hz = 3f₁: the third harmonic.
mcqs.working: One fixed end (node) and one free end (antinode): λ_n = 4L/n with n odd. First harmonic: λ₁ = 4 × 0.60 m = 2.40 m, f₁ = 240/2.40 = 100 Hz. Next mode: n = 3, λ₃ = 4 × 0.60/3 = 0.80 m, f₃ = 240/0.80 = 300 Hz.
rationales: A student who assumes every system has harmonics at all whole-number multiples of f₁ gives 2 × 100 = 200 Hz. With a node at one end and an antinode at the other, L must hold an odd number of quarter-wavelengths, so there is no mode at 2f₁.

A student who takes one loop of the pattern as a whole wavelength identifies the mode correctly but reads L = 3λ/4 (one and a half loops) as 1.5λ, so uses λ = 0.60/1.5 = 0.40 m and gets f = 240/0.40 = 600 Hz. Each loop is half a wavelength, so λ = 4L/3 = 0.80 m and f = 300 Hz.

A student who numbers harmonics in order finds the correct wavelength and frequency but calls the mode the second harmonic. The harmonic number is the ratio f/f₁ = 300/100 = 3, so this is the third harmonic; there is no second harmonic.

There is a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end, so L holds an odd number of quarter-wavelengths. The first harmonic has λ = 4L = 2.40 m and f₁ = 100 Hz. The next mode has L = 3λ/4, so λ = 0.80 m and f = 240/0.80 = 300 Hz = 3f₁: the third harmonic.

mcqs.q: A pipe of length 0.68 m is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air in the pipe is 340 m s⁻¹. Which gives, in increasing order, the lowest frequencies at which the air in the pipe resonates?
options: f = 125 Hz and no other
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: A closed end is a displacement node and an open end an antinode, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, … The first harmonic has λ = 4 × 0.68 = 2.72 m and f₁ = 340/2.72 = 125 Hz; only odd harmonics exist, giving 125, 375 and 625 Hz.
mcqs.working: Closed end: node; open end: antinode. λ_n = 4L/n, n odd. λ₁ = 4 × 0.68 m = 2.72 m; f₁ = 340 m s⁻¹/2.72 m = 125 Hz. f₃ = 3 × 125 = 375 Hz; f₅ = 5 × 125 = 625 Hz.
rationales: A student who assumes all whole-number harmonics exist, as for a string fixed at both ends, gives 125, 250, 375 Hz. With a node at one end and an antinode at the other, only odd multiples of 125 Hz can occur.

A closed end is a displacement node and an open end an antinode, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, … The first harmonic has λ = 4 × 0.68 = 2.72 m and f₁ = 340/2.72 = 125 Hz; only odd harmonics exist, giving 125, 375 and 625 Hz.
A student who treats the closed end as a displacement antinode has an antinode at each end, so uses λ₁ = 2L = 1.36 m and gets 250, 500, 750 Hz. The closed end is a node, so λ₁ = 4L and f₁ = 125 Hz.
A student who thinks a pipe has a single natural frequency gives only 125 Hz. The air column has a series of natural frequencies, one for each odd harmonic: 125, 375, 625 Hz, …

mcqs.q: A lightly damped mass–spring system has a natural frequency of 2.0 Hz. It is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude with a frequency of 3.5 Hz. Which describes its oscillation once the amplitude has become steady?
options: At 3.5 Hz, with a smaller amplitude than when driven at 2.0 Hz
At 2.0 Hz, its natural frequency, with a small steady amplitude
At 3.5 Hz, with a larger amplitude than when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
At 3.5 Hz, with the same amplitude as when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
mcqs.explain: In the steady state a forced oscillator moves at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. The amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency (2.0 Hz, resonance) and smaller away from it.
mcqs.working: Steady forced oscillation is at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. Driving at 2.0 Hz equals the natural frequency (resonance), so the amplitude at 3.5 Hz is smaller than at 2.0 Hz.
rationales: In the steady state a forced oscillator moves at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. The amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency (2.0 Hz, resonance) and smaller away from it.
A student who thinks a driven system keeps oscillating at its natural frequency picks this. Once the transient dies away, the system follows the driving force and oscillates at 3.5 Hz.

A student who thinks faster pushing always gives a larger amplitude picks this. Above the natural frequency the force is increasingly out of step with the motion; the amplitude is largest at resonance, near 2.0 Hz.

A student who thinks the amplitude depends only on the size of the driving force picks this. For a force of fixed size, the amplitude depends strongly on the driving frequency and is greatest at resonance.

mcqs.q: A singer shatters a wine glass by singing one steady note close to it. Which condition is essential for this to happen?
options: The note is very loud, whatever frequency the singer chooses.
The note is the highest frequency that the singer is able to produce.
The note's frequency is equal to a natural frequency of the glass.
The sound echoes inside the bowl of the glass and builds up.
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
mcqs.explain: This is resonance. At a natural frequency of the glass, the sound pushes the glass in step with its own vibration, so energy builds up cycle after cycle until the amplitude is large enough to break the glass.
rationales: A student who thinks a large vibration needs only a large force picks this. A loud note at the wrong frequency drives the glass out of step with its natural vibration, so the amplitude stays small; the frequency must match.

A student who thinks a higher driving frequency always gives a larger amplitude picks this. The amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency equals a natural frequency of the glass, not when it is as high as possible.

This is resonance. At a natural frequency of the glass, the sound pushes the glass in step with its own vibration, so energy builds up cycle after cycle until the amplitude is large enough to break the glass.
A student who uses "resonance" in its everyday sense of echoing picks this. Reflection of sound is not what breaks the glass; the glass itself is driven at one of its natural frequencies.

mcqs.q: A radio receiver contains a circuit whose natural frequency can be adjusted. Signals from many stations, each broadcasting at a different frequency, reach its aerial at the same time. How does the receiver pick out one station?
options: It responds most strongly to the strongest signal, whatever its frequency.
It responds most strongly to the signal with the highest frequency reaching it.
It oscillates at its own natural frequency, whatever signals reach the aerial.
Its natural frequency is set equal to that station's frequency, so it resonates with it.
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
mcqs.explain: This is a useful application of resonance. The circuit responds with a large amplitude only to a signal at (or very near) its natural frequency, so adjusting that frequency to match one station selects it while the others produce only small responses.
rationales: A student who thinks the size of the response depends only on the size of the driving force picks this. A tuned circuit responds strongly to a signal at its natural frequency, even if that signal is weaker than others.

A student who thinks a higher driving frequency always produces a larger amplitude picks this. The response is greatest when the signal frequency matches the circuit's natural frequency, not when it is highest.

A student who thinks a driven system always oscillates at its natural frequency picks this. The circuit is driven by the signals and oscillates at their frequencies; it responds strongly only to the one that matches its natural frequency.

This is a useful application of resonance. The circuit responds with a large amplitude only to a signal at (or very near) its natural frequency, so adjusting that frequency to match one station selects it while the others produce only small responses.

mcqs.q: A lightly damped oscillator is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude, and its steady amplitude is measured over a range of driving frequencies. The damping is then increased slightly, and the measurements are repeated. Which describes the new response curve compared with the first?
options: The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly higher frequency.
The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly lower frequency.
The maximum amplitude is unchanged, and it occurs at the same frequency.
The amplitude falls by the same factor at every frequency; the peak frequency is unchanged.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
mcqs.explain: With more damping, more energy is dissipated per cycle, so the energy balance at resonance is reached at a smaller amplitude. The peak also moves slightly to a lower frequency and becomes wider. This holds provided the damping is still light, as it is after a slight increase.
rationales: A student who thinks damping makes a system stiffer picks this. Damping opposes the velocity; it does not act like a stiffer spring. The frequency of maximum amplitude moves slightly lower, not higher.

With more damping, more energy is dissipated per cycle, so the energy balance at resonance is reached at a smaller amplitude. The peak also moves slightly to a lower frequency and becomes wider. This holds provided the damping is still light, as it is after a slight increase.

A student who thinks the driver simply makes up any losses picks this. The maximum amplitude is reached when the energy supplied per cycle equals the energy dissipated per cycle; with more damping this happens at a smaller amplitude.

A student who thinks damping scales the whole response curve down picks this. Damping acts mainly near resonance: far from the natural frequency the amplitude is almost unchanged, while the peak becomes lower and wider and moves to a slightly lower frequency.

mcqs.q: The same oscillator is driven by a periodic force of the same constant amplitude in two experiments, X and Y, with different damping. In X the maximum amplitude is 25 mm, at 5.00 Hz, and the amplitude falls to half this value at 4.82 Hz and 5.17 Hz. In Y the maximum amplitude is 3.4 mm, at 4.89 Hz, and the amplitude falls to half this value at 3.3 Hz and 6.1 Hz. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: X is more heavily damped, because its peak is at the higher frequency.
Only X shows resonance; Y's damping is too heavy for resonance to occur.
Y is more heavily damped, so at 1.0 Hz its amplitude is also only about a seventh of X's.
Y is more heavily damped: its peak is lower, wider and at a slightly lower frequency.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
mcqs.explain: All three features of Y point to heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude (3.4 mm against 25 mm), a much wider peak (2.8 Hz between the half-maximum points against 0.35 Hz), and a peak at a slightly lower frequency (4.89 Hz against 5.00 Hz).
rationales: A student who thinks damping raises the resonant frequency picks this. Damping moves the peak slightly lower, and X's tall, narrow peak shows light damping; Y is the more heavily damped.

A student who thinks resonance needs an unlimited amplitude picks this. Y's amplitude has a clear maximum of 3.4 mm at 4.89 Hz and falls to half of it on either side: Y resonates too, with a lower, wider peak.

A student who thinks damping scales the whole response curve down by the peak ratio (25/3.4 ≈ 7) picks this. Damping acts mainly near resonance, where it limits the amplitude; far below resonance the amplitude is set mainly by the spring and the size of the force, so at 1.0 Hz the two amplitudes would be almost the same.

All three features of Y point to heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude (3.4 mm against 25 mm), a much wider peak (2.8 Hz between the half-maximum points against 0.35 Hz), and a peak at a slightly lower frequency (4.89 Hz against 5.00 Hz).

mcqs.q: A mass–spring system is displaced from equilibrium and released. Which statement about the effect of damping on its motion is correct?
options: Heavy damping: no oscillation, but a slower return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
Heavy damping: no oscillation, and a quicker return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
Critical damping: it passes through equilibrium once, then comes to rest at equilibrium.
Light damping: the time period decreases steadily as the amplitude of oscillation decreases.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
mcqs.explain: Heavy damping is greater than critical damping. The system does not oscillate, but the large resistive force slows its return, so it takes longer to reach equilibrium than a critically damped system does.
rationales: Heavy damping is greater than critical damping. The system does not oscillate, but the large resistive force slows its return, so it takes longer to reach equilibrium than a critically damped system does.
A student who thinks more damping always stops the system sooner picks this. Critical damping gives the fastest return without oscillation; heavier damping slows the return.
A student who thinks critical damping allows a single swing picks this. A critically damped system does not pass through equilibrium at all; any overshoot means the damping is light.
A student who thinks a smaller oscillation takes less time picks this. With light damping the amplitude decreases while the time period stays almost constant.

mcqs.q: A door closer damps the motion of a heavy door. With the damping first set low, the door, released from wide open, swings past the closed position and back several times before settling. The damping is then increased in small steps. Which describes how the door's motion changes?
options: The swinging past stops at critical damping; beyond it, the door closes even more quickly.
The swinging past stops at critical damping; beyond it, the door closes more slowly.
At critical damping the door swings past just once, then stops at the closed position.
The door keeps swinging past, by less each time, however much damping is added to it.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
mcqs.explain: As the damping increases, the oscillation dies away faster until, at critical damping, the door no longer swings past the closed position and reaches it in the shortest time. Heavier damping than this makes the door creep shut more slowly.
rationales: A student who thinks more damping always brings a system to rest sooner picks this. Beyond critical damping the resistive force slows the door's return, so it takes longer to close.

As the damping increases, the oscillation dies away faster until, at critical damping, the door no longer swings past the closed position and reaches it in the shortest time. Heavier damping than this makes the door creep shut more slowly.
A student who thinks critical damping allows one swing picks this. At critical damping the door does not pass the closed position at all; a door that swings past even once is still lightly damped.
A student who has only seen lightly damped oscillations picks this. At and beyond critical damping the door returns to the closed position without swinging past it.

mcqs.q: A pipe is open at both ends. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Which statement about the motion of the air is correct?
options: The air at the midpoint of the pipe does not oscillate.
The air at each open end oscillates side to side across the pipe.
The air at each open end of the pipe does not oscillate.
The air oscillates with the same amplitude all along the pipe.
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: Each open end is a displacement antinode and, in the first harmonic of a pipe open at both ends (L = λ/2), there is a single displacement node midway along the pipe. At the node the displacement of the air is zero at all times, so the air there does not oscillate.
rationales: Each open end is a displacement antinode and, in the first harmonic of a pipe open at both ends (L = λ/2), there is a single displacement node midway along the pipe. At the node the displacement of the air is zero at all times, so the air there does not oscillate.

A student who reads the standing-wave diagram as a picture of the air's motion picks this. The open ends are indeed antinodes, but the curves drawn across the pipe only show how large the displacement is at each position. Sound is longitudinal, so the air oscillates along the pipe's axis, not across it.

A student who thinks every end is a node, as the ends of a guitar string are, picks this. The air at an open end is free to move, so each open end is a displacement antinode, where the air oscillates with the greatest amplitude. The node of the first harmonic is midway along the pipe.

A student who thinks every point on a standing wave has the same amplitude picks this. The amplitude varies along the pipe: greatest at the open ends (antinodes) and zero at the midpoint (the node), where the air does not oscillate.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the envelope of a standing wave on a string of length L = 1.20 m that is fixed at both ends. What is the wavelength of the waves on the string?
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: Three loops fit between the fixed ends. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so each loop is λ/2: 1.20 m = 3 × λ/2, giving λ = 0.80 m. This is the third harmonic of the string.
mcqs.working: The envelope has three loops between the fixed ends. Each loop (node to node) is half a wavelength, so L = 3λ/2 and λ = 2L/3 = 2 × 1.20 m / 3 = 0.80 m.
rationales: A student who takes one loop, from a node to the next node, as a whole wavelength picks this: 1.20 m / 3 = 0.40 m. One loop is only half a wavelength, because the string bulges the other way in the next loop; a whole wavelength spans two loops, so λ = 0.80 m.
Three loops fit between the fixed ends. Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so each loop is λ/2: 1.20 m = 3 × λ/2, giving λ = 0.80 m. This is the third harmonic of the string.

A student who counts the four nodes (including the ends) and calls the pattern the fourth harmonic, with λ = 2L/4, picks this. The harmonic number is the number of loops, three, not the number of nodes: λ = 2L/3 = 0.80 m.

A student who thinks adjacent nodes are a quarter of a wavelength apart picks this: 4 × 0.40 m = 1.60 m. It is a node and the next antinode that are λ/4 apart; adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, so λ = 2 × 0.40 m = 0.80 m.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal string held between two fixed supports, one at each end, with the distance between the supports marked L = 1.20 m. The standing-wave envelope is drawn as three equal loops between the supports: a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve that touch the dashed equilibrium line at the two supports and at two equally spaced points between them, and are furthest apart at the middle of each loop.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the displacement envelope of the air in a pipe of length L = 0.85 m that is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the sound?
options: 600 Hz
300 Hz
200 Hz
385 Hz
mcqs.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
mcqs.explain: The envelope shows a node at the closed end, an antinode a quarter-wavelength in, a node at the half-wavelength point and an antinode at the open end: the pipe holds three quarter-wavelengths, so λ = 4L/3 = 1.13 m and f = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.
mcqs.working: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode. The pattern has a node at the closed end, one more node inside the pipe and an antinode at the open end, so L = 3λ/4: λ = 4L/3 = 4 × 0.85 m / 3 = 1.13 m. f = v/λ = 340 m s⁻¹ / 1.133 m = 300 Hz (the third harmonic of the pipe).
rationales: A student who takes the full loop between the two nodes as a whole wavelength (and the last quarter of the pattern as half a wavelength) gets L = 3λ/2, λ = 0.567 m and f = 600 Hz. A loop from node to node is half a wavelength, so L = 3λ/4 and f = 300 Hz.

The envelope shows a node at the closed end, an antinode a quarter-wavelength in, a node at the half-wavelength point and an antinode at the open end: the pipe holds three quarter-wavelengths, so λ = 4L/3 = 1.13 m and f = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.

A student who counts the two nodes and calls the pattern the second harmonic, f = 2 × v/(4L), gets 200 Hz. A pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics; with three quarter-wavelengths in the pipe this is the third harmonic, f = 3 × v/(4L) = 300 Hz.
A student who multiplies the speed by the wavelength, f = vλ = 340 × 1.13, gets 385 Hz. Frequency is speed divided by wavelength: f = v/λ = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal pipe drawn as a shaded rectangle with a thick wall at the left end, labelled closed end, and no wall at the right end, labelled open end; the length between the ends is marked L = 0.85 m. Inside the pipe the displacement envelope is drawn as a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve. They meet on the dashed centre line at the closed end and again at a point two thirds of the way along the pipe, and are furthest apart one third of the way along and at the open end, where the envelope ends wide open.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the envelope of a standing wave on a string of length L, driven by a vibrator at its left end and fixed at its right end. The amplitude of the vibrator is so small that both ends of the string can be treated as nodes. P and Q are points on the string. At one instant, P has its maximum displacement, upward. Which describes Q at that instant?
options: Q is displaced upward by exactly the same amount as P.
Q is moving through its equilibrium position.
Q is displaced upward but by a smaller amount than P.
Q is displaced downward by the same amount as P.
mcqs.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
mcqs.explain: P and Q are the same distance from the node at the midpoint, so they have equal amplitudes, and they lie in adjacent loops, on opposite sides of that node, so they oscillate in antiphase. When P is at its maximum displacement upward, Q is at its maximum displacement downward, and the two displacements are equal in size.
rationales: A student who thinks the whole string moves up and down together picks this. Points in adjacent loops are in antiphase: while the left-hand loop bulges upward the right-hand loop bulges downward, so Q is displaced downward when P is displaced upward.

A student who applies the travelling-wave rule Δφ = 2πx/λ picks this: P and Q are λ/4 apart (λ = L here), giving a phase difference of π/2, so Q would be at zero displacement when P is at its maximum. In a standing wave all points within one loop are in phase and points in adjacent loops are in antiphase, so Q is at its maximum displacement, downward, at that instant.

A student who pictures the wave weakening as it travels away from the vibrator, with the string rising and falling as one, picks this. The amplitude of a point on a standing wave depends only on its distance from the nearest node: P and Q are the same distance from the midpoint node, so their amplitudes are equal, and because they lie in adjacent loops they oscillate in antiphase, so Q is displaced downward by the same amount as P is displaced upward.

P and Q are the same distance from the node at the midpoint, so they have equal amplitudes, and they lie in adjacent loops, on opposite sides of that node, so they oscillate in antiphase. When P is at its maximum displacement upward, Q is at its maximum displacement downward, and the two displacements are equal in size.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal string running from a small box labelled vibrator at the left to a fixed support at the right. The standing-wave envelope has two equal loops: a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve that meet on the dashed equilibrium line at both ends and at the midpoint of the string. A dimension line below marks the two halves of the string as L/2 and L/2. Two red dots on the equilibrium line mark points P and Q: P is a quarter of the way along the left-hand loop from the midpoint node, and Q the same distance to the right of the midpoint node in the right-hand loop.

mcqs.q: The graph shows how the steady amplitude of a lightly damped mass–spring system depends on the frequency of the periodic force that drives it. The amplitude of the driving force is kept constant while its frequency is reduced slowly from 8.0 Hz to 2.0 Hz. Which describes the amplitude of the mass–spring system during this change?
options: It falls throughout, because a slower driving force transfers less energy to the system.
It stays the same throughout, because the amplitude of the driving force does not change.
It rises to a maximum as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz, then falls again.
It rises to a maximum near 5 Hz then stays there, as the system now oscillates at its natural frequency.
mcqs.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
mcqs.explain: The graph peaks at about 5 Hz, the natural frequency of the system. As the driving frequency falls from 8.0 Hz it approaches the natural frequency and the amplitude grows, is largest when the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance), and then decreases again as the driving frequency moves further below the natural frequency towards 2.0 Hz.
mcqs.working: The peak of the response curve, read from the graph, is at about 5 Hz: this is the natural frequency of the system. Reducing the driving frequency from 8.0 Hz brings it towards 5 Hz, so the amplitude rises; it is greatest as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance) and then falls as the driving frequency continues down to 2.0 Hz.
rationales: A student who thinks a faster driver always gives a bigger response picks this. The amplitude depends on how close the driving frequency is to the natural frequency, not on how high it is: the graph rises as the frequency comes down towards 5 Hz and only falls once the frequency is below that.

A student who thinks the size of the response is set only by the size of the force picks this. With the same force amplitude the response varies strongly with frequency, as the graph shows: small far from 5 Hz and largest at resonance.

The graph peaks at about 5 Hz, the natural frequency of the system. As the driving frequency falls from 8.0 Hz it approaches the natural frequency and the amplitude grows, is largest when the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance), and then decreases again as the driving frequency moves further below the natural frequency towards 2.0 Hz.

A student who thinks a driven system settles at its own natural frequency picks this: once the driver has passed 5 Hz the system is imagined to keep resonating on its own. After the transient dies away a driven system oscillates at the driving frequency, whatever that is; the graph shows that when the driving frequency has fallen to 2.0 Hz the steady amplitude is small again.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis, marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10). The curve starts at a small amplitude at low frequency, rises slowly at first and then steeply to a single sharp peak close to 5 Hz, then falls steeply and flattens out towards a very small amplitude by 8 Hz and beyond.

mcqs.q: Curve X on the graph shows how the steady amplitude of a driven oscillator varies with driving frequency. One change is then made to the apparatus, and the measurements are repeated to give curve Y. Which change was made?
options: The damping acting on the oscillator was made smaller.
The amplitude of the driving force was reduced.
The natural frequency of the oscillator was lowered.
The damping acting on the oscillator was increased.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
mcqs.explain: Curve Y has the three signs of heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude, a wider peak, and a peak at a slightly lower frequency. Away from resonance the curves coincide, which is also expected, because damping matters most near resonance, where the amplitude is limited by the energy dissipated per cycle.
rationales: A student who thinks damping makes a system stiffer, raising its resonant frequency, reads the lower peak frequency of Y as a sign of less damping. Damping lowers the peak frequency slightly, and Y's lower, broader peak confirms that the damping was increased.

A student who thinks damping cannot alter the steady amplitude of a driven system looks for another cause and blames the driver. A smaller driving force would scale the whole curve down, including the parts far from resonance, and would not shift or broaden the peak. Only Y's peak region differs from X, which is the effect of increased damping.

A student who thinks damping scales the whole response curve down rules damping out, because the curves coincide away from the peak, and attributes the small shift to a change in the natural frequency. A lower natural frequency would move the whole peak, not make it three times lower and much broader; a lower, broader peak at a slightly lower frequency is the signature of increased damping.

Curve Y has the three signs of heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude, a wider peak, and a peak at a slightly lower frequency. Away from resonance the curves coincide, which is also expected, because damping matters most near resonance, where the amplitude is limited by the energy dissipated per cycle.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8) with two curves. Curve X, blue, has a tall narrow peak at 4 Hz and falls steeply to small amplitudes on either side. Curve Y, red, has a peak about one third as high as X's, much broader, and centred slightly below 4 Hz. At frequencies well below the peaks (under about 2 Hz) and well above them (over about 6 Hz) the two curves almost coincide.

mcqs.q: The graph shows displacement–time curves X, Y and Z for the same mass–spring system, released from rest at the same displacement with three different amounts of damping. Which statement about the curves is correct?
options: Y shows heavy damping: the heaviest damping gives the quickest return to equilibrium.
X shows critical damping: it crosses equilibrium once and then settles at it.
Y shows critical damping: it reaches equilibrium in the least time without crossing it.
X shows heavy damping: even heavy damping leaves a small oscillation before rest.
mcqs.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
mcqs.explain: Critical damping is the smallest damping for which the system returns to equilibrium without oscillating, and it gives the quickest return. Y is on the axis sooner than Z and, unlike X, does not cross it, so Y is critically damped; X is lightly damped and Z heavily damped.
rationales: A student who thinks more damping always brings a system to rest sooner picks this. Beyond critical damping the resistive force slows the return, which is why Z creeps back more slowly than Y. Y, the quickest non-oscillating return, shows critical damping and Z shows heavy damping.

A student who thinks a critically damped system overshoots once picks this. A critically damped system does not cross equilibrium at all. Any crossing, even a single small one, means the damping is less than critical, so X shows light damping.

Critical damping is the smallest damping for which the system returns to equilibrium without oscillating, and it gives the quickest return. Y is on the axis sooner than Z and, unlike X, does not cross it, so Y is critically damped; X is lightly damped and Z heavily damped.

A student who thinks every damped system oscillates a little before it stops picks this. With critical or heavy damping the system returns to equilibrium without crossing it, as Y and Z do; X, which crosses the axis and dips below it, is the lightly damped case.

figure.alt: Graph of displacement x (vertical axis) against t / s (horizontal axis marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8). All three curves start at the same positive displacement at t = 0. Curve X, blue, falls, crosses the time axis at about 2.8 s, dips a little below it, and then returns to the axis, on which it lies from about 6.5 s onwards. Curve Y, red, falls smoothly to the axis without crossing it and is almost on it by about 5 s. Curve Z, dashed, falls more slowly than Y, never crosses the axis, and is still clearly above it at 8 s.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Physics (guide first assessment 2025, updated November 2023); topic C.4 Standing waves and resonance
topicGuidance: The formation of standing waves from the superposition of more than two waves should not be considered.
Pipes will be referred to as open or closed.
End corrections for open pipes are not required.
Boundary conditions for strings include two fixed boundaries, one fixed and one free boundary, and two free boundaries.
Boundary conditions for air in pipes include two closed ends, one closed and one open end, and two open ends.
Vibration modes of air in pipes will be discussed in terms of displacement nodes and antinodes.
For standing waves in air, pressure nodes and antinodes are not required.
The lowest frequency mode of a standing wave will be referred to as the first harmonic. The terms fundamental and overtone are not to be used in this course.
A determination of the wavelength and the frequency of the nth harmonic given the length of the string or pipe and the speed of the wave is required.
Only a qualitative analysis is required concerning the impact of damping on the frequency response of a driven oscillator.
Knowledge of the useful and destructive effects of resonance is required.

scopeNotes.statement: The formation of standing waves from the superposition of more than two waves should not be considered.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every standing wave in the items and concepts is formed from exactly two identical travelling waves moving in opposite directions (on a string, the incident and reflected waves). No item or concept combines three or more waves.

scopeNotes.statement: Pipes will be referred to as open or closed.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Pipes are described only as open or closed at each end ("closed at one end and open at the other", "open at both ends"); no other names for pipes are used.

scopeNotes.statement: End corrections for open pipes are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every pipe calculation takes the displacement antinode to be exactly at the open end, so the pipe length is used directly in λ = 4L/n or λ = 2L/n; no end correction appears in any stem, working or distractor.

scopeNotes.statement: Boundary conditions for strings include two fixed boundaries, one fixed and one free boundary, and two free boundaries.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The concepts give the node/antinode rule and the harmonic series for all three string boundaries; items test two fixed boundaries (q06) and one fixed and one free boundary (q07). The misconception that every end is a node (m11) is tested on open pipe ends (q05, q16).

scopeNotes.statement: Boundary conditions for air in pipes include two closed ends, one closed and one open end, and two open ends.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The concepts give the harmonic series for air in pipes with two closed ends, one closed and one open end, and two open ends; items test the closed–open pipe (q05, q08), the case in which the boundary conditions change the harmonic series, and the pipe with two open ends (q16).

scopeNotes.statement: Vibration modes of air in pipes will be discussed in terms of displacement nodes and antinodes.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every node and antinode in air is a displacement node or antinode, and the motion of the air is described as a longitudinal displacement along the pipe (q16 tests this directly).

scopeNotes.statement: For standing waves in air, pressure nodes and antinodes are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item, concept or misconception refers to pressure nodes or antinodes; the closed-end misconception (m12) is explained and corrected in terms of the displacement of the air only.

scopeNotes.statement: The lowest frequency mode of a standing wave will be referred to as the first harmonic. The terms fundamental and overtone are not to be used in this course.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The lowest-frequency mode is called the first harmonic throughout, and higher modes are named by harmonic number n (so the second mode of a closed–open pipe is the third harmonic). The two banned terms appear only in verbatim quotations of the guidance (topicGuidance, the S03 guidance field and this note's statement); no concept, misconception, stem, option or rationale uses them.

scopeNotes.statement: A determination of the wavelength and the frequency of the nth harmonic given the length of the string or pipe and the speed of the wave is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Three items require the nth harmonic from the length and the wave speed: q07 asks for both λ and f (a string with one fixed and one free end), while q06 (a string with two fixed ends) and q08 (a pipe closed at one end) ask for f, with λ found as a step in the working.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the useful and destructive effects of resonance is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: One destructive effect (a glass shattered by a sustained note, q10) and one useful effect (tuning a radio receiver, q11) are tested, and the concept c16 lists further useful and destructive examples.

scopeNotes.statement: Only a qualitative analysis is required concerning the impact of damping on the frequency response of a driven oscillator.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Damping is treated only qualitatively: the peak of the frequency response becomes lower, wider and moves to a slightly lower frequency. The data in q13 are read comparatively (the only arithmetic is the ratio of the two given peak amplitudes, in one distractor); no damping coefficient, equation for the response curve or calculated amplitude is used.
